planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil; give it room to develop its broad canopy away from walkways where dropping fruit can stain pavement.

directions: This old European bird cherry selection is grown for its exceptionally long, pendant racemes of fragrant white flowers, noticeably longer than those of the wild species, which open in mid-spring before the leaves fully expand. Small black cherries follow and are quickly stripped by birds, so expect mess rather than a harvest if planted over paving. It grows into a broad, round-headed tree that tolerates wet soil and cold better than most ornamental flowering cherries, making it a good choice for streamside or northern plantings where other Prunus struggle. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing damaged wood, ideally right after flowering.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, where light levels keep the purple foliage color from fading toward green.

directions: Unlike the white-flowered species, this selection opens pale pink blossoms against new foliage that emerges deep purple-bronze and matures to a purplish green, giving two seasons of color rather than one. Small dark cherries ripen in summer among the colored leaves, adding further contrast before birds clean them off. It keeps the same rounded, medium-sized tree habit and cold hardiness as the wild bird cherry, so it fits into mixed borders or as a specimen where a true species tree would otherwise be chosen. Full sun produces the strongest foliage color, while deep shade causes the purple cast to wash out.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil; its narrow upright form suits tight side yards or street-tree plantings where a spreading bird cherry would not fit.

directions: This older German selection keeps a distinctly narrower, more upright crown than the typically broad-headed wild bird cherry, while still carrying the same heavy spring display of fragrant white, pendant flower racemes. The tighter habit makes it far more useful in confined urban plantings or narrow borders than the species, without sacrificing bloom quality. Small black cherries follow in summer and attract birds quickly, so plant it away from patios and walkways. It shares the species' tolerance for cold, wet soil, and needs little pruning beyond removing any wayward branches that threaten the upright shape.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; give it room to spread outward since it stays very low to the ground.

directions: A Colorado selection of native sand cherry valued for an extremely flat, mat-forming habit that stays under two feet tall while spreading six to eight feet wide, making it one of the lowest true groundcover shrubs available for cold, dry climates. White flowers wreath the branches in early spring, followed by small dark purple-black cherries that are edible but mostly left for birds. It is exceptionally tolerant of drought, wind, and poor sandy or gravelly soil, making it a strong choice for slope stabilization or xeriscape plantings where turf or perennials would need far more water. Little pruning is required beyond occasionally thinning crowded growth from the center of older plants.
